## P-values {#sec-p-values}

```{r}
#| label: setup-3-2
#| include: false
source(if (file.exists("R/setup.R")) "R/setup.R" else "../R/setup.R")

# z statistics from earlier examples, rounded as in those examples
two_prop_z <- function(x1, n1, x2, n2) {
  p1 <- x1 / n1; p2 <- x2 / n2
  pbar <- round((x1 + x2) / (n1 + n2), 4)
  se0 <- round(sqrt(pbar * (1 - pbar) * (1 / n1 + 1 / n2)), 4)
  round((p1 - p2) / se0, 3)
}
z_debt  <- two_prop_z(171, 300, 165, 250)    # Example 3.1.1, H1: p1 != p2
z_brand <- two_prop_z(58, 200, 36, 180)      # Your Turn 3.1.1, H1: pA > pB
z_wage  <- round((358.4 - 380) / 10, 3)      # Example 2.1.1, H1: mu < 380
z_card  <- two_prop_z(84, 240, 96, 240)      # Exercise 3.1.2, H1: p1 < p2
z_cop   <- round((148 / 400 - 0.30) / round(sqrt(0.30 * 0.70 / 400), 4), 3)  # Example 2.3.1, H1: p > 0.30
```

### Learning Objectives

1. Explain what a p-value is.
2. Find the p-value of a $z$ test from Table 4 for a left-sided, right-sided or two-sided test.
3. Make the decision of a test with the p-value, and check that it agrees with the critical region.

### Concept

So far we have decided by checking whether the test statistic falls in the
**critical region**. A second way, used by all statistical software, is the
**p-value**.

::: {.callout-important icon=false}
## p-value

The **p-value** is the probability, assuming $H_0$ is true, of getting a test
statistic at least as extreme as the one we observed, in the direction(s) of $H_1$.

A small p-value means our sample would be unusual if $H_0$ were true.

**Decision rule:** reject $H_0$ if p-value $< \alpha$; accept $H_0$ if p-value $\ge \alpha$.
:::

The p-value is an **area beyond the test statistic**, in the direction of $H_1$:

| $H_1$ | p-value |
|:---:|:---|
| $<$ | area to the **left** of the test statistic |
| $>$ | area to the **right** of the test statistic |
| $\ne$ | **twice** the area beyond the test statistic in one tail |

```{r}
#| label: fig-pval-z
#| layout-ncol: 3
#| fig-cap: "The p-value as an area under the z curve (orange)"
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - "H1: <"
#|   - "H1: >"
#|   - "H1: ≠"
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-width: 3.3
pval_plot(-1.5, "left", "z")
pval_plot(1.5, "right", "z")
pval_plot(1.5, "two", "z")
```

The critical-region method and the p-value method always give the **same
decision**: $z_{\text{cal}}$ falls in the critical region exactly when the
p-value is less than $\alpha$.

::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## What the p-value is not

The p-value is **not** the probability that $H_0$ is true. It is calculated
assuming $H_0$ is true.
:::

### Finding a p-value from the $z$ Table

Table 4 gives the area to the **left** of a positive $z$. To find a p-value:

1. Round $|z_{\text{cal}}|$ to 2 decimals and read the area to its left, $P(Z \le |z_{\text{cal}}|)$.
2. The area in one tail beyond it is $1 - P(Z \le |z_{\text{cal}}|)$.
3. Take one tail for a one-sided test (in the direction of $H_1$), or twice that area for a two-sided test.

The p-value is rounded to 4 decimals.

```{r}
#| label: ex-3-2
e <- pz_table(z_debt, "two")
```

### Example

**Example 3.2.1.** In Example 3.1.1 (household debt, urban vs rural) we
tested $H_0: p_1 = p_2$ against $H_1: p_1 \ne p_2$ and found
$z_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(z_debt, 3)`$. Find the p-value and make the decision at
$\alpha$ = 0.05. Compare with the critical-region method.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=false}
## Solution

The test is two-sided, so the p-value is the area in **both** tails beyond
$\pm`r fmt(abs(z_debt), 3)`$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ex-3-2
#| fig-cap: "p-value for Example 3.2.1: the two tails beyond ±2.153"
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-align: center
pval_plot(z_debt, "two", "z")
```

From Table 4, $P(Z \le `r fmt(e$a, 2)`) = `r fmt(e$F, 4)`$, so one tail is
$1 - `r fmt(e$F, 4)` = `r fmt(e$tail, 4)`$ and
$$
\text{p-value} = 2(`r fmt(e$tail, 4)`) = `r fmt(e$p, 4)`.
$$

The test in five steps, with the p-value in Step 4:

**Step 1: Hypotheses.** $H_0: p_1 = p_2$ $\quad H_1: p_1 \ne p_2$

**Step 2: Level of significance.** $\alpha$ = 0.05

**Step 3: Test statistic.** $z_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(z_debt, 3)`$ (from Example 3.1.1)

**Step 4: p-value.** p-value = `r fmt(e$p, 4)`

**Step 5: Decision and interpretation.** p-value = `r fmt(e$p, 4)` < $\alpha$ =
0.05, so we reject $H_0$. That is, the proportion of households with debt is
different in urban and rural areas at the 0.05 level of significance.

| Method | Comparison | Decision |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Critical region (Example 3.1.1) | $z_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(z_debt, 3)` < `r fmt(-crit_z(.975), 3)`$ | reject $H_0$ |
| p-value | p-value = `r fmt(e$p, 4)` < 0.05 | reject $H_0$ |

Both methods give the same decision.
:::

```{r}
#| label: yt-3-2
y1 <- pz_table(z_brand, "right")
y2 <- pz_table(z_wage, "left")
```

### Your Turn

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Your Turn 3.2.1

Find the p-value from Table 4 and make the decision at $\alpha$ = 0.05.

(a) Your Turn 3.1.1 (brand switching): $H_1: p_A > p_B$, $z_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(z_brand, 3)`$.
(b) Example 2.1.1 (construction wages): $H_1: \mu < 380$, $z_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(z_wage, 3)`$.
:::

```{r}
#| label: curves-3-2-1
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-subcap: ["", ""]
#| fig-height: 1.8
#| fig-width: 3.6
blank_curve("z"); blank_curve("z")
```

::: {.workspace lines="8"}
:::

::: {.answer title="Your Turn 3.2.1"}
(a) Right-sided: p-value = area to the right of $`r fmt(z_brand, 3)`$.
$P(Z \le `r fmt(y1$a, 2)`) = `r fmt(y1$F, 4)`$, so p-value $= 1 - `r fmt(y1$F, 4)` = `r fmt(y1$p, 4)`$.
p-value = `r fmt(y1$p, 4)` < $\alpha$ = 0.05, so we reject $H_0$ (the same decision as in Your Turn 3.1.1).

(b) Left-sided: p-value = area to the left of $`r fmt(z_wage, 3)`$. By symmetry it equals
the area to the right of `r fmt(abs(z_wage), 2)`: $1 - `r fmt(y2$F, 4)` = `r fmt(y2$p, 4)`$.
p-value = `r fmt(y2$p, 4)` < $\alpha$ = 0.05, so we reject $H_0$ (the same decision as in Example 2.1.1).
:::

### Formula Summary

| | |
|:---|:---|
| p-value | probability, assuming $H_0$ is true, of a test statistic at least as extreme as observed, in the direction of $H_1$ |
| From Table 4 | one tail $= 1 - P(Z \le |z_{\text{cal}}|)$; one-sided: p-value = one tail (in the direction of $H_1$); two-sided: p-value = 2 × one tail |
| Decision | reject $H_0$ if p-value $< \alpha$; accept $H_0$ if p-value $\ge \alpha$ |

```{r}
#| label: ex-3-2-exercises
x1 <- pz_table(z_cop, "right")
x2 <- pz_table(z_card, "left")
```

### Exercises

**3.2.1** Find the p-value from Table 4 and make the decision at $\alpha$ = 0.05.

(a) Example 2.3.1 (co-payment scheme): $H_1: p > 0.30$, $z_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(z_cop, 3)`$.
(b) Exercise 3.1.2 (price displays): $H_1: p_1 < p_2$, $z_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(z_card, 3)`$.

::: {.answer title="Exercise 3.2.1"}
(a) Right-sided: p-value $= 1 - P(Z \le `r fmt(x1$a, 2)`) = 1 - `r fmt(x1$F, 4)` = `r fmt(x1$p, 4)`$ < 0.05: reject $H_0$.

(b) Left-sided: p-value $= P(Z \le `r fmt(z_card, 3)`) = 1 - P(Z \le `r fmt(x2$a, 2)`) = 1 - `r fmt(x2$F, 4)` = `r fmt(x2$p, 4)`$ $\ge$ 0.05: accept $H_0$.

Both agree with the critical-region decisions in Sections 2.3 and 3.1.
:::

**3.2.2** For each p-value, write the decision at $\alpha$ = 0.05:
(a) 0.0312, (b) 0.0500, (c) 0.1847, (d) 0.0005.

::: {.answer title="Exercise 3.2.2"}
(a) 0.0312 < 0.05: reject $H_0$.
(b) 0.0500 $\ge$ 0.05: accept $H_0$.
(c) 0.1847 $\ge$ 0.05: accept $H_0$.
(d) 0.0005 < 0.05: reject $H_0$.
:::

**3.2.3** A student says: "The p-value is 0.03, so there is a 3% chance that
$H_0$ is true." Explain what is wrong.

::: {.answer title="Exercise 3.2.3"}
The p-value is calculated assuming $H_0$ is true. It is the probability of a
result at least as extreme as the sample result if $H_0$ were true, not the
probability that $H_0$ is true.
:::
